Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) is the initial and rate-limiting enzyme of pyrimidine catabolism and clears the large majority of administered 5-FU to inactive dihydrofluorouracil. Partial or complete DPD deficiency, usually from DPYD variants, markedly raises and prolongs 5-FU exposure so that a standard dose behaves as an overdose and shunts more drug into the anabolic pathway.

nodes.description: FUTP is incorporated into cellular RNA in place of UTP, disrupting RNA processing and function. This RNA-directed toxicity is largely independent of the thymidylate pathway; that uridine triacetate, which delivers competing uridine, rescues toxicity is clinical evidence for an RNA-directed component, though the point is inferred from the antidote's effect rather than shown directly here.

Excess circulating 5-FU accumulates either from an absolute overdose (classically an ambulatory-infusion-pump error compressing a multi-day dose into hours) or from a standard dose in a patient whose catabolic clearance is impaired. 5-FU and its oral prodrug capecitabine both converge on the same circulating active drug.

The exposure is iatrogenic: 5-FU, or capecitabine (its oral prodrug), is given as cancer chemotherapy to large numbers of patients. Poisoning follows when that administration is excessive (an overdose or infusion-pump error) or when a standard dose is not cleared because of DPD deficiency.

nodes.description: FdUMP forms a stable ternary complex with thymidylate synthase and the folate cofactor 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate, blocking de novo synthesis of dTMP. The resulting dTTP depletion and nucleotide-pool imbalance drive uracil misincorporation, futile excision-repair cycling and DNA strand breaks ("thymineless death"). Thymidylate synthase is the sole de novo source of thymidylate and the principal target of 5-FU.
